title: The Loop That Never Ends: Sizes Are Unsigned, and Arithmetic Does Not Care

questions.question: A std::vector<double> is empty. What is readings.size() - 1?
options: 18446744073709551615, the largest number a std::size_t can hold
-1, since 0 minus 1 is minus one
0, because sizes cannot go below zero
Undefined behaviour, so anything at all
questions.explanation: Sizes are unsigned, and unsigned arithmetic wraps rather than going negative. It is a defined result, not undefined behaviour, which is why it is so hard to find: the program carries on with a perfectly good number that is wrong.

questions.question: Why does for (std::size_t i = v.size() - 1; i >= 0; --i) never finish?
options: Nothing unsigned is ever less than zero, so the condition cannot become false, and --i at zero wraps to the largest value
Because v.size() is re-evaluated every pass and keeps changing
It does finish, but only after 2^64 passes
Because --i on an unsigned value is undefined behaviour
questions.explanation: Measured over a three element vector with a cap: still running after ten passes. The wrap at the bottom is the mechanism, and it is defined behaviour, so no sanitiser reports it either.

questions.question: int missing = -1; is missing < readings.size() true, for a vector of three?
options: No: the -1 converts to unsigned first and becomes larger than any size
Yes: -1 is less than 3
Yes, but only on a 64 bit machine
It is undefined, so it depends on the compiler
questions.explanation: (std::size_t)(-1) is 18446744073709551615, so the comparison is false. The answer flips relative to reading it as arithmetic. gcc, clang and MSVC all warn about this one, which makes it the friendly half of the problem.

questions.question: Under -Wall -Wextra, which of these does the compiler say nothing about?
options: v[v.size() - 1], on both gcc and clang
int i < v.size(), on both
-1 < v.size(), on both
All of them warn on both compilers
questions.explanation: The diagnostics cover the comparisons, cover them inconsistently between compilers, and say nothing at all about the arithmetic. size() - 1 is the dangerous one and it is the one nothing mentions.

questions.question: gcc reports the unsigned countdown through -Wtype-limits and clang does not. What follows from that?
options: A project that builds on one compiler is relying on a net with a known hole in it
clang is wrong and should be reported upstream
The code is only a bug when compiled with gcc
Nothing: warnings are advisory and both are equally safe
questions.explanation: This is why the curriculum builds every lesson on gcc, clang and MSVC. The same code is not diagnosed the same way, and finding out which compiler notices what is not something to discover in a release.

questions.question: You want the last element of a container that might be empty. What is the safest thing to write?
options: Check it is not empty, then use back(), which does no arithmetic at all
readings[readings.size() - 1], which is the standard idiom
readings[last_index(readings.size())], which handles the empty case
readings.at(readings.size() - 1), which throws if it is wrong
questions.explanation: last_index is right for driving a countdown loop, and it still gives -1 here, which is not an index. The version with no arithmetic in it cannot have an arithmetic bug, and that is worth more than any check bolted onto one that does.
